papers.title: Time of Day Dependent Effectiveness of Anti-IgE Therapy in Asthma: Clinical and Experimental Evidence
papers.abstract: BackgroundAsthma is a time-sensitive inflammatory disease whose activity exhibits daily (circadian) rhythms. An outstanding question is whether such temporal variations extend to advanced asthma treatments like biologics that are used for moderate-to-severe disease. ObjectiveTo examine how time-of-administration relates to the effectiveness of the anti-IgE biologic, omalizumab. MethodsWe performed a retrospective cohort study of omalizumab effectiveness in 153 patients with asthma with timestamped administration records. Time of day was modeled as a continuous variable and dichotomized into morning (8:00-11:59, n=74) versus afternoon (12:00-17:00, n=79) administration. Multivariable logistic regression and Cox time-to-event analyses were used to adjust for key covariates. For biological validation, we treated ovalbumin (OVA)-sensitized mice with anti-IgE antibody at various times of day and measured its impact on inflammatory lung pathology. ResultsReceiving the initial dose of omalizumab in the afternoon was associated with better response, defined as a 50% or more reduction in asthma exacerbations in the year after initiation (Odds ratio, OR: 5.20; 95% CI, 1.94-13.96). For each hour later in the day the initial dose of omalizumab was given, the odds of a response increased by 34% (adjusted OR, 1.34; 1.02-1.77). In OVA-sensitized mice, anti-IgE treatment attenuated inflammatory lung pathology, including OVA-induced airway hyperresponsiveness and type-2 inflammation-related gene expression, in a time-of-day-sensitive manner, with maximum effectiveness when dosed in the latter part of the dark phase, functionally analogous to the afternoon in humans. ConclusionThe timing of anti-IgE treatment for asthma may influence therapeutic success. These findings have implications for optimizing the effectiveness of respiratory biologics. Take-home messagesO_LIIgE-targeted therapy in patients with asthma and in murine experimental asthma varied in effectiveness based on administration time. C_LIO_LIIn patients, receiving the first omalizumab dose in the PM (vs. AM) was associated with better treatment response. C_LI

papers.title: Timing the Target: Exploring the Circadian Transcriptome of Biologic Therapies in Asthma.
papers.abstract: Background: Many of the immune pathways involved in asthma or in asthma treatment show circadian or diurnal variation. Understanding this variation can aid in biomarker discovery and/or therapy optimization. Objective: To evaluate if receptors, cytokines, and their pathways (n=46) targeted by currently approved biologics show significant diurnal rhythmicity and to identify their peak expression time. Methods: We used longitudinal bulk RNA sequencing datasets (discovery/replication cohorts: GSE113883 and GSE223613) and one microarray file (GSE39445) for cross-platform replication/validation. First, we used 16 canonical clock genes (including CLOCK, BMAL1, REV-ERB-beta) as positive controls to explore rhythmicity in each cohort. Thereafter, we evaluated if any targets of currently approved biologics or their corresponding receptors showed significant diurnal variation. For significant genes (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR<0.05), we estimated the baseline average, phase, peak-time of expression across the 24-hour day using clock time and quantified the cross-cohort consistency in the peak time of expression across the cohorts. Results: These cohorts included 453 longitudinal samples collected every two to four hours over a 24-28h cycle. Twelve (75%) of 16 evaluable clock genes showed significant rhythmicity. Only 34 of 46 (74%) asthma-related genes were evaluable across two or more cohorts. Of these 34 genes, 23 (68%) showed significant variation. Across all cohorts, the most preserved rhythmically expressed targets included many pathways or targets of monoclonal antibodies that are currently approved or in development: GATA3 and STAT6, master regulators of type 2 inflammation and IL4/IL13 signaling; chemokines, including the neutrophil chemoattractant, CXCL8; IL-5RA, benralizumab's target; FcRE1, suppressed by omalizumab; and IL1RL1(ST2) in clinical trials. Conclusion: Many therapeutic targets in asthma show significant diurnal rhythmicity. Future studies on how dosing time affects their therapeutic effectiveness while minimizing side effects are needed.

papers.title: WakeSentry: real-time awakening detection from single-channel EEG across sleep cohorts and forehead headbands
papers.abstract: Objective/Background: Awakenings after sleep onset are a core measure of sleep continuity, and EEG headbands and closed-loop stimulators, now used at home, must detect each one as it happens, to count it or to stop stimulation. Open sleep stagers match expert scorers, yet have been evaluated only offline over whole nights, so their real-time performance is untested. Patients/Methods: To fill this gap, we developed WakeSentry, which reads only past frontal EEG and learns the moment of waking through an awakening module. We tested it on 1,529 nights from five polysomnography (PSG) cohorts, three clinical, each held out of training, and on 224 headband nights, against GSSC, U-Sleep and YASA. Results: At a matched rate of 0.5 false awakenings per hour, WakeSentry caught more awakenings than GSSC in every cohort and on both headbands. On PSG its sensitivity rose from 63.8% to 70.5%, above U-Sleep and YASA on average. On the headbands it rose from 49.8% to 53.9%, a gain lost without the awakening module. With thresholds preset on the training cohorts, it still outperformed GSSC in six of seven test sets, with at most 0.40 false awakenings per hour. As a replayed stimulator gate, it shortened stimulation during wake in five test sets while staying open for at least 85% of N2 and N3. Conclusions: WakeSentry therefore works in patients and on unseen headbands. It can count awakenings at home and stop stimulation at each one, enabling multi-night monitoring of insomnia and closed-loop stimulation that stops when the sleeper wakes.

papers.title: Validity and reliability of the SSF Preschoolers' Activity Questionnaire (SSF-PAQ) for assessing active play, screen time, and sleep in Japanese preschool children
papers.abstract: Background: The parent-reported Sasakawa Sports Foundation Preschoolers' Activity Questionnaire (SSF-PAQ) is from a national survey of Japanese preschoolers' out-of-preschool exercise, active play, screen time, and sleep. We assessed the validity, reliability, measurement error, paper-electronic agreement, and practicality of the Original version and explored a 24-hour version (SSF-PAQ-24). Methods: Children aged 3-6 years from 10 conveniently sampled preschools wore an accelerometer for seven days while parents kept a time-use diary and completed the SSF-PAQ on Days 7 and 10. Criteria were accelerometer-measured physical activity (PA), diary-recorded screen time, and diary- and accelerometer-derived night sleep. Results: The concurrent-validity sample comprised 167 children (Original, 127; SSF-PAQ-24, 40). Original-version correlations were weak for organized PA and active play ({rho} = 0.24) and moderate-to-vigorous PA ({rho} = 0.29) but strong for screen time ({rho} = 0.83) and night sleep ({rho} = 0.78), which averaged 8.2 and 10.7 min/day above the criteria. Test-retest intraclass correlations were 0.78-0.96 for these measures and 0.27-0.89 for setting-specific items. Screen time was higher on paper than electronically. SSF-PAQ-24 activity correlations were not significant ({rho} = 0.17 and 0.06). Completion took 6.5-9.7 minutes. Conclusion: The Original SSF-PAQ's main measures showed good-to-excellent test-retest reliability, and screen time and night sleep correlated strongly with the criteria. Activity-time validity was limited but comparable to that of existing parent-report questionnaires. SSF-PAQ-24 activity items need re-examination in a larger sample.

papers.title: Early Time-Restricted Eating Reduces Fat Mass In Morning Chronotype Adults With Overweight/Obesity
papers.abstract: Time-restricted eating (TRE) is a promising strategy to improve weight management and metabolic health, but its efficacy may vary depending on the coherence between the eating window and individual chronotype. In a randomized 12-week intervention of morning chronotype adults with overweight or obesity, early TRE (06:00h-14:00h) led to greater reductions in body fat mass compared to late TRE (12:00h-20:00h) and active control (three meals per day). Continuous glucose monitoring revealed enhanced circadian glucose rhythmicity and increased glycemic variability in early TRE, whereas postprandial glucose excursions were attenuated in late TRE. Early TRE induced the most pronounced systemic multi-omic changes, characterized by distinct transcriptional and metabolic programs, including reduced triglyceride and increased sphingomyelin levels. We found that in morning chronotype, early TRE and late TRE elicit distinct adaptations in body composition, glucose and lipid metabolism, and altered transcriptional and metabolic signatures. ClinicalTrials.gov registration no. NCT04618133.

papers.title: Two Axes of Sleep, One Heart: Dissociating Objective Sleep-Disordered Breathing From Subjective Sleep Duration in Cardiac Risk
papers.abstract: Background: Cardiovascular epidemiology has long treated "sleep" as a single exposure, although it denotes both an objective physiological state and a subjective behaviour. We tested whether these domains carry separable information about cardiac risk. Methods and Results: We derived an objective axis from 8,444 polysomnograms (Sleep Heart Health Study) and a subjective axis of self-reported duration from 407,303 adults in the 2020 and 2022 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System. Multivariable regression (n=213,489), quadratic dose-response modelling, sleep-stratified comorbidity networks, and era-stratified tests were combined. Objective sleep-disordered breathing was continuous and right-skewed (median apnea-hypopnea index, 31.8 events/h; median sleep efficiency, 69%) in a risk-enriched cohort. Both short (<7 h) and long (>9 h) sleep were associated with disease after full adjustment: adjusted odds ratios for heart attack were 1.24 (95% CI, 1.19-1.30) and 1.30 (1.19-1.42), and for stroke 1.12 (1.06-1.17) and 1.42 (1.29-1.57). A positive quadratic term confirmed a U shape for all 4 outcomes formally tested (P[≤]6.3x102), with fitted nadirs of 7.26 to 7.85 hours. Suboptimal sleep also raised comorbidity-network density from 0.089 to 0.112 (short sleep; +26%) and 0.108 (long sleep; +22%), with non-overlapping bootstrap CIs and concordant effects across demographic strata. A survey-weighted replication in official CDC microdata (n=344,010; median design effect, 4.43) preserved the principal cardiac, U-shaped, and network findings; an exploratory COVID-19 interaction (P=0.020) did not survive design-based correction. Conclusions: Objective breathing pathology and subjective duration are separately prognostic, and suboptimal sleep amplifies the cardiometabolic comorbidity network. Duration alone cannot exclude asymptomatic sleep-disordered breathing; cardiovascular prevention should assess both axes.

papers.title: Imaging and Motor Asymmetry in Parkinson's Disease associated with GBA and LRRK2 mutations: Data from the PPMI study
papers.abstract: Background: According to the -Synuclein Origin site and Connectome (SOC) model, idiopathic Parkinson's Disease (iPD) is classified into two distinct subtypes: symmetric body-first, with diffuse spread and early non-motor clinical manifestations, and asymmetric brain-first, with initially circumscribed motor manifestations. Evidence regarding the application of this model to genetic PD remains limited. Objective: To investigate imaging and motor asymmetry in genetic vs iPD and idiopathic REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (iRBD), addressing thus indirectly the SOC model in genetic PD. Methods: We analyzed demographic, imaging and clinical data from 85 GBA PD, 166 LRRK2 PD, and 912 iPD patients, as well as 30 iRBD participants with abnormal DATSCAN from the PPMI database. Imaging asymmetry was assessed both by Asymmetry Index and absolute Asymmetry difference. Motor asymmetry was calculated as the absolute difference between the MDS-UPDRS III scores of the right and left sides. Results: GBA- and LRRK2-PD patients exhibit more symmetric putaminal radioligand uptake than iPD patients, but greater imaging asymmetry than iRBD subjects in the caudate. iRBD is more symmetric than iPD in both caudate and putamen. Consistent with the imaging data, GBA- and LRRK2-PD exhibit greater clinical motor symmetry than iPD. Conclusion: GBA- and LRRK2-PD are more symmetric than iPD on imaging and clinical grounds. GBA-PD appears to be a predominantly symmetric diffuse synucleinopathy, as predicted by the SOC model. The SOC model may not be applicable to LRRK2-PD, with its predominantly circumscribed motor phenotype, possibly because in this case -Synuclein pathology does not determine lateralization of motor manifestations.

papers.title: Real-World Cuff-Measured Blood Pressure Trajectories in 20,003 Consumer Wearable Users
papers.abstract: Consumer wearables increasingly allow users to log cuff-measured blood pressure (BP), but resulting BP trajectories are uncharacterized. In this retrospective cohort study, 20,003 adults with Elevated BP or Stage 1 or Stage 2 Hypertension logged BP via a consumer wearable platform. We modeled 6-month trajectories with linear mixed-effects models and examined associations of [≥]5 mmHg reduction with engagement and wearable-derived metrics. Adjusted systolic reductions ranged from -2.6 mmHg (95% CI -3.1 to -2.2) in Elevated BP to -12.1 mmHg (-12.5 to -11.7) in Stage 2 Hypertension; diastolic reductions were -3.7 and -9.2 mmHg in Stage 1 and Stage 2. Overall, 50.2% achieved a [≥]5 mmHg systolic reduction and 27.9% reached normal BP. App time, journaling, AI Coach use, and BP logging were associated with higher odds of reduction; longer sleep and greater physical activity accompanied lower BP. These associational findings support consumer wearables as potentially scalable BP-monitoring platforms.

papers.title: ProbeFit: one-seizure qualification and personalisation of multimodal wearable seizure detectors
papers.abstract: Background and Objective: Missed seizures hinder assessment of seizure frequency and treatment. Although wearables can detect seizures automatically, performance varies between patients. Before deployment, it remains difficult to identify suitable patients, and personalisation usually requires several recorded seizures. We propose ProbeFit to predict later seizure sensitivity and personalise a wearable detector from the first recorded seizure. Methods: We used multicentre SeizeIT2 recordings of behind-the-ear EEG, ECG, EMG and movement from 125 patients. Two generic detectors' peak responses to the first seizure generated a qualification probability. The same seizure and preceding background personalised the detector. ProbeFit was developed on 96 patients and applied unchanged to 29 held-out patients. Expert-labelled video-EEG seizures provided the reference. Evaluation compared qualification with the first-seizure heart-rate rule and measured discrimination, calibration and net benefit, and it compared later sensitivity of the generic and personalised detectors at equal false-alarm rates. Results: Among 27 held-out patients with 152 later seizures, qualification correlated with later sensitivity at Spearman {rho} = 0.38, with one-sided p = 0.033. It identified patients with later sensitivity [≥] 0.5 with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.74. Across all 97 evaluable patients, AUC was 0.76 against 0.59 for the heart-rate rule, a difference of 0.17 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.05 to 0.29. At the qualification threshold of 0.5, ProbeFit withheld deployment from 9 of 15 held-out patients below the sensitivity criterion, and its net benefit was 0.074 against -0.111 for selecting everyone. At equal false-alarm rates between 0.25 and 2 per day, personalisation raised later sensitivity by 2.2 percentage points in held-out patients and by 6.3 points in development patients. Both confidence intervals excluded zero, and no held-out patient lost sensitivity. Conclusions: ProbeFit uses the first recorded seizure to predict whether a wearable detector will detect at least half of a patient's later seizures, and it personalises that detector without waiting for further seizures. It supports patient selection and adaptation during the first monitoring admission.

papers.title: Changes in Health Behaviors and Correlational Patterns among High School Students Across Two Longitudinal Studies
papers.abstract: Purpose - This study examines whether six health behaviors remain stable among high school students across the school year and whether associations between these behaviors recur across assessments. Design/methodology/approach - As part of a school health program evaluation, a pre-post longitudinal health survey was conducted among two samples of high school students in a U.S. vocational-technical high school. Study 1 surveyed 114 students from late winter to late spring in 2024. Study 2 surveyed 177 students from autumn 2024 to late spring 2025. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests examined group-level behavioral change, and Pearson correlation networks described associations among six health behaviors: sleep, breakfast consumption, physical activity, nature exposure, social media use, and mindfulness practices. Findings - The primary analyses detected no significant group-level changes in any of the six behaviors across either study interval, suggesting relative stability within these samples. A one-time survey may provide useful information for broad school health planning, whereas repeated assessment remains necessary for evaluating longer-term patterns or program effects. Sleep and breakfast showed the most consistent positive association. Physical activity and nature exposure were positively associated at three of the four assessments. Social media was isolated from the other behaviors at the first three assessments but was negatively associated with sleep and physical activity at the final assessment. Originality - The study distinguishes stability in group-level behavior from changes in the relationships among behaviors. The findings support efficient assessment for broad educational planning. They also identify behavior pairs that can be addressed together in school health education, including sleep and breakfast, physical activity and nature exposure, and social media, sleep, and physical activity.

papers.title: Validity and reliability of the Japanese version of the Movement Behaviour Questionnaire-Child (MBQ-C) for assessing active play, screen time, and sleep in preschool children
papers.abstract: Background: Valid and feasible measures of preschoolers' 24-hour movement behaviours are needed for population-level research. We developed a Japanese version of the Movement Behaviour Questionnaire-Child (MBQ-C) and evaluated its measurement properties and practicality. Methods: After translation and cross-cultural adaptation following the COSMIN procedure, including cognitive interviews, we evaluated the questionnaire in a cross-sectional validation study of Japanese children aged 3-6 years. Concurrent validity was assessed against hip-worn accelerometry and a 7-day diary; we also examined test-retest reliability, measurement error, agreement between response formats and modes, and practicality (completion time, burden, and clarity). Analyses used Spearman correlations, intraclass correlation coefficients, the SEM, smallest detectable change (SDC), and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results: Of 208 children, 170 provided valid accelerometer and diary data for the concurrent-validity analysis, and 187 completed the MBQ-C for the questionnaire-based analyses. Concurrent validity was weak for active and energetic play (Spearman {rho} = 0.12-0.26), strong for total screen time (0.78-0.85), and moderate for total sleep (0.48-0.58). Test-retest reliability was moderate to good (ICC, 0.66-0.81), and within-child variability was lowest for sleep (CV 3%) and highest for the physical activity items (21-33%). The open- and closed-ended versions showed no significant differences; paper-electronic agreement was good for screen time and sleep but poor for active play. Completion took approximately 6-9 minutes, with low reported burden. Findings were robust in sensitivity analyses. At the group level, SDC for a mean was SDCind/{surd}N: 119.8/{surd}N, 74.0/{surd}N, 112.6/{surd}N, and 92.5/{surd}N min/day for active play, energetic play, total screen time, and total sleep, respectively (N = number of children surveyed). The systematic differences between the two test-retest occasions were +15.7, +6.5, +4.0, and -5.4 min/day, respectively. Conclusions: The Japanese MBQ-C is a practical option for assessing preschoolers' active play, screen time, and sleep at the group level. By quantifying its group-level measurement error, this study provides benchmarks for interpreting group-level differences and change, supporting the use of the MBQ-C in surveillance and evaluation of programmes delivered at scale.

papers.title: A report-supervised EEG-language foundation model enables broad, interactive clinical interpretation
papers.abstract: Medical AI for complex signals such as electroencephalography (EEG) relies on costly expert annotations and predefined diagnostic labels that fail to capture the richness and nuance of clinical interpretation. Whether models trained on routine clinical reports can overcome these limitations while matching expert-supervised performance remains unclear. We introduce EEG Copilot, a biosignal-language foundation model trained on routine EEG-report pairs without dedicated task-specific expert annotations. Across two external datasets (6,078 EEGs), EEG Copilot performed on par with a state-of-the-art expert-supervised model across 11 shared findings (mean AUROC 0.80-0.81), corroborated by direct neurologist review of 200 EEGs. Beyond predefined diagnostic categories in conventional EEG AI, EEG Copilot assessed 23 clinical characteristics through natural-language questions in English and German across 9,689 EEGs from four hospitals (mean AUROC 0.80-0.82), demonstrating that automated EEG assessment need no longer be confined to fixed diagnostic outputs. Crucially, EEG Copilot generated integrated clinical impressions directly from EEG rather than isolated predictions with shuffled-report controls supporting recording-specific content and neurologist review of 800 impressions showing that most were accurate or clinically usable with minor errors. These findings chart a path beyond label-bound medical AI, transforming routine clinical reports into scalable supervision for flexible, language-driven assessment and integrated interpretation of complex physiological signals.

papers.title: Exploring the genetic determinants of ALS in a North Indian cohort using a genomic screening approach
papers.abstract: Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a clinically and genetically heterogenous neurodegenerative disorder in which both monogenic and complex genetic mechanism contribute to disease susceptibility. Increasing evidence also indicates that non motor manifestations, including sleep disturbances, significantly influence disease burden. This study aimed to characterize the genetic spectrum of ALS in a predominantly North Indian cohort while evaluating the prevalence of sleep related abnormalities. Methods: Seventy-three clinically diagnosed ALS patients were recruited from a tertiary care centre in North India. Disease severity was assessed using the ALSFRS-R. Sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, and REM sleep behaviour disorder symptoms were evaluated using the PSQI, ESS and RBDQ questionnaires, respectively. Genetic analysis included targeted sequencing of SOD1, TARDBP, and ANG, followed by repeat expansion analysis of C9orf72, ATXN1, ATXN2, ATXN3, and ATXN7. Whole exome sequencing was performed in selected cases to further investigate the genetic basis of ALS. Results: The cohort demonstrated a male predominance and an earlier age of onset compared to many Western populations. Poor sleep quality and excessive daytime sleepiness were frequently observed although no significant association was found between sleep parameters and disease severity. Genetic screening identified a pathogenic/likely pathogenic TARDBP variant classified by ClinVar while no known or novel pathogenic variants were detected in SOD1 or ANG. Repeat expansion studies revealed one patient harbouring pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansions. For the ATXN1, one patient harboured pathogenic repeat expansions and two patients carried intermediate length repeats. Additionally, one patient harboured intermediate repeat expansions in ATXN2. Whole exome sequencing revealed novel and rare variants in ALS associated genes including ANXA11, SIGMAR1, SETX, ERBB4 and NEK1, highlighting substantial genetic heterogeneity. Conclusions: Our findings highlight the complex genetic heterogeneity of ALS, with pathogenic repeat expansions and rare variants identified across multiple disease associated genes. These results demonstrate the importance of comprehensive genetic testing to improve the detection of clinically relevant variants in ALS. In addition, the high prevalence of sleep related disturbances observed in the cohort emphasizes the need to incorporate non motor assessment into routine clinical evaluation of patients with ALS.

papers.title: The ACROSSS-study. The role of sleep characteristics before and after a cardiovascular event. Rationale and study design.
papers.abstract: Studies of myocardial infarction and stroke showed a diurnal variation with peaks in the morning and afternoon. So far, night sleep or napping have not been investigated as triggers for cardiovascular events via a case-crossover study. Therefore, the main question of the ACROSSS (Acute CoROnary Syndrome, Stroke and Sleep) study is how much the occurrence of a myocardial infarction/stroke/transient ischemic attack is associated with taking a nap shortly before (topic 1, case-crossover study, 656 patients needed). Moreover, the study aims at assessing the incidence of sleep disturbances three and twelve months after a myocardial infarction/stroke/transient ischemic attack (topic 2, follow-up study, 400 patients needed). Recruitment of patients is carried out in four German hospitals in Essen and Bottrop, North Rhine-Westphalia. The examination program includes the case-crossover questionnaire on potential acute triggers of cardiovascular events, a sleep questionnaire with validated instruments (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, etc.) and a questionnaire on health status and lifestyle habits. Moreover, eligible patients are screened for sleep apnea and during the follow-up sleep is measured by actigraphy. The combination of sleep-related and clinical data offers a deeper understanding of how sleep affects the acute onset of a cardiovascular event and recovery afterwards.

papers.title: Targeting memory consolidation in major depression via pharmacological slow-wave sleep promotion
papers.abstract: Slow-wave sleep (SWS) has been implicated in memory consolidation and brain plasticity and proposed as a therapeutic target in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, whether pharmacological promotion of SWS causally improves memory consolidation remains unknown. Gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), a robust enhancer of SWS, represents a promising drug-repurposing candidate to target this pathway. We therefore conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 22 patients with MDD and 20 matched healthy controls receiving single nocturnal doses of GHB, trazodone as an active comparator, or placebo under polysomnographic monitoring (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04082806). Declarative, procedural and emotional memory were assessed before and after sleep. GHB strongly increased SWS duration and delta power, whereas trazodone produced smaller changes in sleep-stage composition. Contrary to our hypothesis, neither drug improved memory consolidation across domains. Exploratory analyses revealed weak associations between global sleep-stage measures and memory, alongside selective associations with spindle and spectral features. These findings challenge the assumption that increasing SWS alone is sufficient to improve overnight memory consolidation and suggest that more targeted modulation of sleep oscillatory dynamics may be required.

papers.title: Motherly Plus: Study Protocol of a Randomized Controlled Trial Evaluating a Smartphone-Assisted Single-Session Psychotherapy Intervention for Postpartum Depression
papers.abstract: Introduction: Postpartum depression (PPD) is a public health problem, affecting approximately 17% of women worldwide. PPD is associated with significant costs to the healthcare system and impairments for the child. Although evidence shows that psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy are effective in reducing PPD symptoms, access to these treatments is limited, especially in low- and middle-income countries where there is a shortage of professionals and unequal distribution of mental health services. In this context, telehealth, smartphone apps, and brief psychotherapies emerge as viable, low-cost, and potentially scalable alternatives. However, gaps remain regarding the efficacy of single-session psychotherapies for PPD, especially when combined with digital support. Objectives: The primary objective is to test the efficacy of an intervention package combining single-session psychotherapy with subsequent self-guided use of a smartphone app for the treatment of PPD. Secondary objectives are to investigate moderators, mediators, and specific intervention processes. Method: A randomized clinical trial in which 104 women aged 18-40 years, up to 12 months postpartum, with a diagnosis of PPD will be randomized to the intervention (single-session psychotherapy supported by the Motherly app) or a waitlist. Participants in the intervention arm will retain access to the app throughout the study; waitlist participants will receive the intervention after post-treatment assessment. Assessments will occur at T1 (week 1, baseline), T2 (week 2, mid-treatment), T3 (week 4, post-treatment), and T4 (week 8, follow-up). The primary outcome will be depression assessed by the QIDS-C16 at T3. Secondary outcomes include anxiety, sleep, parental stress, and self-reported depression. Data will be analyzed using generalized estimating equations (GEE) models considering an intention-to-treat (ITT) perspective. Mediation models will be used to analyze mediators, while interaction models will be used to explore potential moderators. Regression models will be used to analyze the association between specific processes (therapeutic alliance and app engagement) and clinical outcomes. Perspectives: This study has potential public health relevance and innovation by testing an intervention package that combines single-session psychotherapy and technology, with high potential for scalability. Trial registration: clinicaltrials.gov NCT07925762 Key words: Postpartum depression; clinical trial; cognitive-behavior therapy; digital intervention; smartphone app; single session psychotherapy

papers.title: Impaired cortical gap-mediated inhibition in chronic tinnitus but with limited individual diagnostic accuracy
papers.abstract: Tinnitus lacks an objective marker, limiting diagnosis and treatment evaluation. We tested whether gap-mediated inhibition of cortical sound-evoked responses provides one. In a prospective, multicentre case-control study at seven sites in the United States and Europe, adults with and without chronic tinnitus heard brief pulses preceded or not by a silent gap, embedded in broadband or narrowband carriers, during electroencephalography. The primary outcome was inhibition of the N100 response. Of 584 eligible participants, 455 yielded high-quality recordings with complete covariate data (232 cases, 223 controls; mean age 45.4 years, 52% women) that entered the adjusted analyses. Inhibition was strongest for broadband noise whereas narrowband carriers gave limited dynamic range. Participants with tinnitus showed reduced broadband gap-mediated inhibition ({beta} = -19.27%, d = -0.413, cluster-corrected p = 0.002), scaling with tinnitus severity (covariate-adjusted {surd}THI model: partial R2 = 0.049, p = 0.0015). In contrast, discrimination of individuals was limited (AUC 0.612, 95% CI 0.560-0.663). Cortical gap inhibition is a reproducible group-level effect rather than an individual diagnostic test.

papers.title: Childhood sleep trajectories, hypomanic symptoms, and cognitive functioning in early adulthood: a longitudinal cohort study
papers.abstract: Background Sleep and circadian rhythm disturbances are implicated in bipolar disorder (BD), yet it remains unclear whether developmental trajectories of sleep and circadian rhythms across childhood confer risk for hypomanic symptoms (HS) and cognitive dysfunction. Here, we examined whether distinct sleep duration and sleep timing trajectories across childhood are associated with potential HS and cognitive functioning in early adulthood. Methods Using data from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC), parent-reported night-time sleep duration and mid-point of sleep (MPS) from 6 months to 11 years were modelled using latent class growth analysis. During the ALSPAC study, HS were assessed at ages 21 to 23 using the Hypomania Checklist (HCL), and cognitive functioning (working memory and response inhibition) was assessed at age 24. Results Four sleep duration and three MPS trajectories were identified. Logistic regression analyses showed that persistently average shorter (OR=2.87, 95% CI=1.31 to 6.32) and persistently longer sleep (OR=2.81, 95% CI=1.08 to 7.30) trajectories were associated with increased risk of potential HS, while persistently earlier MPS was associated with lower odds (OR=0.23, 95% CI=0.11 to 0.49). Multiple linear regression models showed that experiencing HS in combination with persistently average shorter sleep was associated with poorer response inhibition (B=36.55, 95% CI=8.33 to 64.78, p=0.011), whereas HS in combination with persistently longer sleep was associated with better response inhibition (B=-125.21, 95% CI= -193.56 to -56.86, p<0.001). No interactions were found for working memory. Conclusions Persistently average shorter and persistently longer sleep duration trajectories were associated with increased risks of experiencing HS, as measured by the HCL, while earlier circadian timing were associated with reduced risks. Differences in early-life sleep regulation may be associated with subsequent risk of experiencing HS during early adulthood and may differentially shape subsequent response inhibition performance. Keywords: hypomania; sleep; trajectories; cognition; ALSPAC

papers.title: Altered oscillatory coupling and a candidate inhibitory circuit mechanism in Rett syndrome
papers.abstract: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused primarily by pathogenic variants in the MECP2 gene and characterized by severe cognitive and neurological impairment. Phase amplitude coupling (PAC), a cross-frequency interaction supporting information integration across temporal and spatial scales, provides a window into large-scale neural coordination and circuit dysfunction. PAC depends on coordinated activity among specific neuronal subtypes, yet the cellular mechanisms shaping oscillatory dynamics in RTT remain poorly understood. Here we combined electroencephalography (EEG) with biophysically constrained computational modeling to characterize PAC alterations and investigate their circuit-level origins. Awake resting-state EEG was recorded from 42 individuals with RTT and 37 typically developing participants, and PAC strength was quantified. Individuals with RTT exhibited stronger PAC across widespread frequency pairs and cortical regions, including elevated theta gamma coupling in posterior, midline, and whole brain regions, and elevated alpha gamma coupling in anterior, posterior, and whole brain regions. Biophysically constrained network simulations of a cortical Layer 4 model comprising pyramidal neurons together with PV+, SOM+, and VIP+ interneurons demonstrated that reduced excitability of VIP+ interneurons selectively reproduced the increased theta gamma and alpha gamma PAC observed in RTT. These findings identify abnormal PAC as an electrophysiological feature of RTT and suggest a possible mechanistic link between altered oscillatory coordination and VIP+ interneuron dysfunction. PAC may provide a non-invasive marker of inhibitory circuit dysfunction and a translational framework for investigating shared circuit abnormalities across neurodevelopmental disorders.
